title: The Rising Danger of Regional Confrontation
author: Melvin Goodman
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-04-at-4.33.40-PM-680x482.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/05/the-
rising-danger-of-regional-confrontation/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-

Photo by [Edwin
Hooper](https://unsplash.com/@edwinhooper?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText)

With every passing day, the wars in Eastern Europe and the Middle East are
taking on a larger regional cast and threatening to meld. The mindless nature
of the growing confrontation points to more friction on the horizon.

There is a linkage between the Russian-Ukrainian confrontation and the
U.S.-Israeli war against Iran and its surrogates. Last week, Ukraine struck an
Iranian commercial cargo ship in the Caspian Sea that was reportedly taking
military equipment from Iran to Russia. It took diplomatic calls to defuse the
crisis and to dissuade Iran from striking back.

This incident was inevitable in view of Iran’s increasing supply of military
aid, particularly Shahed drones, to Russia. In addition to drones, Iran has
sent drone trainers to Crimea to assist Russian military forces. The Russians,
in turn, are improving the drone technology and sending newer drone versions
to Iran for use against U.S. facilities in Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain.

U.S. intelligence is involved in Ukrainian targeting of Russian forces, and
the Trump administration assumes that Russia is involved in similar activity
on behalf of Iran. The United States, moreover, claims that Iran has provided
ballistic missiles to Russia for use against Ukraine, but this has not been
confirmed.

The U.S.-Israeli invasion of Iran was planned as a short war, but it is
turning into an unmitigated, gale-force cock-up. Fighting continues in the
sixth month and as many as 17 nations may be involved. Iran launched attacks
on U.S. military facilities in Kuwait last week, and an Egyptian port near the
Suez Canal was hit as well. Two ships were hit, including a U.S. gas storage
tanker. These attacks threaten Saudi Arabia’s use of the Red Sea, needed to
gain access to the canal. This was necessitated by the Houthis attacks to
close down the Strait of Bab-el-Mandeb that connects the Red Sea to the Indian
Ocean.

Israel learned nothing from its failed invasion of Lebanon in 1982 that led to
the formation of Hezbollah. Israel didn’t withdraw its forces from southern
Lebanon two decades later. In destroying much of the leadership of Hezbollah,
the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps has taken a greater role in Hezbollah’s
efforts to maintain pressure on Israel.

There are danger signs in Europe as well. Last week, a Russian cruise missile
violated Polish air space and exploded in a rural field in eastern Poland.
Russia has been waging a multi-front “shadow war” against NATO members for the
past year. Romania destroyed three Russian Shahed-type drones last month, and
Moldova has reported Russian penetrations. There have been cyber attacks on
European infrastructure as well as Russian involvement in cutting undersea
data cables in the Baltic and North Seas.

Meanwhile, there is increasing collaboration of nations in Europe and Asia
that no longer have confidence in U.S. credibility. In the Indo-Pacific, Japan
has strengthened defense ties with Australia, the Philippines, and India as
well as with South Korea. Australia has concluded new agreements with several
Pacific Island nations in order to deal with increased Chinese activity in the
region. In Europe, there is greater collaboration between Britain, France, and
Germany as well as between the eastern and western members of NATO. These
arrangements could be difficult to manage, and could foster Russian and
Chinese challenges to protect their interests.

Warfare has its own culture, and it often damages the very civil societies
that support the use of it. When elements of nationalism and fears of
existential threats are introduced, the expansion of force becomes more
likely. Self-defense is typically the justification for going to war, but the
actions of Russia against Ukraine, Israel against Gaza, and the United States
against Iran are excessive. When wars are designed for political gain, it
becomes more difficult to accept negotiation and compromise.
